title: Al-Biruni on fairness
hook: he writes that he will set out the views of others as they are, without distortion (India)
tomorrow: can you fight someone's army and still call some of them friends?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Khaldun on teaching: teach gently. Today, a gentleness that's harder to keep: being fair to people you think are wrong.

A clip goes around: half a sentence from someone on the other side, cut so it sounds ridiculous. The replies pile on. Nobody goes back for the whole sentence. Al-Biruni, a Muslim scholar, opens his book on India in a scene like that. He's with his teacher, and they're reading a writer who describes the beliefs of a Muslim school, the Mu'tazila, and twists them until they look foolish. His teacher is unhappy about it. So he asks al-Biruni for something harder than a reply: write down what the people of India believe, the way they themselves would say it.
screen: `HALF A SENTENCE, CUT TO LOOK DUMB.` → `A TEACHER READS A TWISTED BOOK.` → `WRITE IT THE WAY THEY'D SAY IT.`

segments.voice: So he does. His book sets out Hindu beliefs, books, sciences and customs, and in the preface he names his rule plainly: he will set out the views of others as they are, without distortion. This book, he says, is not a polemic, not an argument against anyone. Where Hindu thinkers say something close to the Greek philosophers, he sets the two side by side so readers can see the likeness. When a belief sounds strange to his Muslim readers, he often separates what the learned hold from what ordinary people say, a line you could draw in any people, his own included. He doesn't hide that he's a Muslim, or that he disagrees in places. He just keeps two jobs apart: first describe, then discuss. He's honest about how hard the first job is. In his opening chapter he names the walls between peoples: language, religion, customs, and old suspicion on both sides. The Qur'an had already set the bar: don't let hatred of a people pull you away from justice. Here's the thing worth telling a friend tonight: a careful account of Hindu thought, written by a Muslim who made fairness the rule. Fair doesn't mean agreeing. It means a Hindu reader could recognize their own belief in your words. Then, and only then, you've earned the right to disagree.
screen: `THE RULE: AS THEY ARE.` · `NOT A POLEMIC.` · `THE WALLS BETWEEN PEOPLES.` · `FIRST DESCRIBE, THEN DISCUSS.` · then, large: `AS THEY ARE.`

segments.voice: Choose one view you disagree with, a real one, from a friend, a relative, or the news. Write it down by hand in one sentence, the way its best defender would put it. Read it back slowly: would they nod?
screen: `ONE VIEW YOU DISAGREE WITH.` · `IN ITS DEFENDER'S WORDS.` · `WOULD THEY NOD?`

segments.voice: Al-Biruni on fairness: a Muslim scholar who wrote down the beliefs of India as their own people held them, and kept his arguments for later.
To keep: as they are, a fair hearing before any answer. Seven stops on the road, one to go.

howItsDone: Muslim students of other religions still read al-Biruni's book on India; teachers who follow him describe another faith from its own books and people before discussing it.

fork.setup: your aunt keeps a strict diet you think is silly. at dinner a cousin asks you why she eats that way. what does al-Biruni's rule ask of you?
options: call it a fad, but kindly, so nobody's feelings get hurt.
give her reasons the way she would, then your view if asked.
change the subject; explaining it could sound like agreeing.
fork.reveal: first describe, then discuss. al-Biruni set out others' views as they are, and only then said where he differed.

original.note: Arabic: insaf, fairness, giving each side its due.

trapdoor: what you thought: fairness means staying neutral and never saying what you think.
what it means: describe a view as its own people hold it, without distortion, then say where you differ.
what a scholar hears: al-Biruni's preface to his book on India (Kitab fi Tahqiq ma li-l-Hind), written after his teacher objected to a writer's twisted account of the Mu'tazila.
guess: describing others' beliefs the way they'd describe them
proving another religion wrong with polite arguments
keeping quiet about any belief you don't share
